findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, so 'what is it' and 'why does it matter' are answered before any scrolling.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The title and heading are about firstmate, a different project, so a newcomer who came to Athena's site may at first think they are on the wrong page. Only the second paragraph explains that the page is a study Athena wrote to show what it can do.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title> / h1 of the same text

findings.text: What to do next is clear. A link near the top jumps to concrete steps: prerequisites, clone, install and a sample one-line request, with a note that it asks before it runs.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the Next steps section: "git clone ...", "./setup.sh", "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: This link sits in the header and speaks to 'your decision', which a first-time visitor does not have. It reads like an internal control and may confuse them about who the page is for.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision"

findings.text: The page describes Athena's main workflow (request, worker model, checker model, cost, commit) only in prose. Everything below shows the study feature instead, so a newcomer never sees what a traced commit or cost record actually looks like.
findings.source: "It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: Most of the page is a detailed state machine of firstmate, covering exit codes, pending-close records and --force semantics. That shows traceability well but is far more than a newcomer needs, and the page gives no signal that they can stop reading after 'Start here'.
The early definitions bring in more firstmate terms (secondmate, captain call, merge authority) before defining them, so the 'Start here' section is harder going than its heading promises.
findings.source: Words used first: "home ... A secondmate is a persistent home of its own, not a task in someone else's backlog."

findings.text: The page tells the reader how to read the citations and lets them check any claim against pinned source lines. This backs up Athena's selling point of being accountable.
findings.source: "Each statement below ends with the id of the claim that supports it; the claims, with links to their sources, are listed at the end."
